I have an older Kenmore d/w, model 665.17462300.
The door latch had worn down over many years of use, so that the detergent compartment wouldn't stay shut.

The dispenser fits and functions well....but only after I swapped out its solenoid for the one in the older model.

The problem is that the connectors at the end of the cable harness do not match the plugs in the new dispenser.
Fortunately, the solenoids themselves were identical, and the old one functioned [the solenoid is a form of electromagnet, which pushes the latch to open the little hatch that contains the detergent].

If you have the right two-pin female socket, you can replace the cable harness pins yourself. Otherwise, just replace the solenoid, with its built-in connectors

Like mentioned by a few, our detergent dispenser had the little tab broken so the lid would not close. These tabs are tiny and fragile. I recommend using it gently or another replacement is in line.

Regarding the unit install: (for the Kenmore dishwasher listed above. Your mileage may vary)
Simple install. Need a T15H torx bit and remove the screws around the edge on the inside panel of the dishwasher. Once removed, the front of the dishwasher comes off. Remove the wires (brown) by gently lifting up the tabs and pull. Once the wires are disconnected, remove the metal bracket - you will see a metal bracket with 6 hex screws that you will need to remove with a 3/16 socket, then pull up the 2 plastic clips on the top/left and bottom/right of the detergent dispenser. Install is simply the reverse.

Tools to have for this job:
- T15H torx bit
- 3/16 hex socket
- flat head or your nails to lift up the 2 plastic tabs on the dispenser

The product was a Whirlpool part for my Kenmore/Sears dishwasher.  The original dispenser had the tab wear out so the detergent lid would not close.  As shown in the photos, the new product had a different connector for power to the actuator motor.  Since the only issue with the old dispenser was the door clasp, I was able to remove the original motor/actuator and place it on the new unit.  The actuator arm can be lifted slightly to remove the motor after the retaining screw is removed.  If the motor on your unit us bad, then you will either need to buy a new connector to splice to your power wires or attempt to solder the power wires directly to the terminal connectors.  That appears to be a tough option given the small size and space in which to solder.  Overall, the part fit and works well.

First off, excellent replacement part.

My washer was throwing a tE code which indicated a thermistor failure. That is the device that checks water temperature in the machine. When I pulled the machine apart (using YouTube as my guide) I discovered that the original gasket had a small tear at its lowest part (adjacent to the drain tube). This was allowing water to seep down and corrode to contact for the thermistor. I cleaned the contacts with a small wire brush, applied some dielectric grease (can be found at Home Depot) and replace the door gasket. Problem solved.

Now, the replacement of the gasket was somewhat difficult but certain well worth the savings of having a repair person come out to fix the machine. The gasket was a perfect match. I am however disappointed with the original gasket. No idea how the tear could have occurred unless it was a defective part to begin with and slowly failed over time with use.

It would have been a bit easier if I had actually taken the washer apart, but I've done that a couple of times and thought I'd save time. I was wrong about that.

One trick I finally stumbled upon after trying about every tool I had to try to get the inner retaining ring on was to take some baling wire I had laying around. I looped it around the spring and the loop in the piece of metal that attaches to the spring. Then taking a pair of lineman pliers, I twisted the ends of the baling wire over and over to expand the spring until I had enough room to slide the hook through it. Once I hit upon this trick, it was a quick process.

As other raters have pointed out, our LG washer was flashing a 'te' thermistor error during certain types of loads. When we took the washer apart, we found a small rip in the rubber boot, just above the heater/thermistor assembly. Since we've replaced the boot, no more error. Looks like the leak was playing havoc with the electronics. One other note; why was there a hole you may ask? Pay attention when you reattach the pinch-clamp to the hose at the bottom of the boot. Make sure the clip is turned in such a way that the sharp edges don't come into contact with the rubber boot. It looks like this was the root cause of the problem.
